text: Spark's query planner picks a physical plan before the query runs, based on statistics that are often stale or wrong for a filtered query. Adaptive Query Execution re-optimizes that plan at runtime, using real measured numbers instead of the upfront guess.

A shuffle plans a fixed number of output partitions upfront. If the real data turns out much smaller, that's a pile of tiny, nearly-empty partitions. AQE measures real sizes after the shuffle and merges the tiny ones into a handful of right-sized partitions.

The planner picks a join algorithm before it knows either side's real size. AQE can switch a planned sort-merge join to a broadcast join after the shuffle, once one side turns out small enough — a choice the upfront plan couldn't safely make.

One oversized partition can become a straggler task the whole job waits on. AQE splits that partition into smaller sub-partitions that run in parallel instead — the direct fix for skew, not something more cluster nodes can solve alone.
Three runtime corrections: coalescing, join switching, skew splitting — all based on real numbers. Next up: caching, and which layer actually helps versus which one just wastes memory.
